text:
Decide what you'll test before you look at the data. Good advice... but how do you know what to test, without looking? Here are two hundred and forty-four restaurant bills, and the tip left on each one. Split them by day, and one stands out. Friday tips best, at seventeen percent... against fifteen on Saturday. But only nineteen of these bills are from a Friday. A group that small wobbles a lot. Swap the average for the median, and Sunday wins instead. So this isn't a finding. It's a lead... a question worth asking properly. Which means there are two different jobs here.

Exploring is roaming the data, slicing it every way you can. What comes out is questions, never conclusions. Confirming is stating ONE hypothesis in advance, and testing it once, on data nobody has looked at. What comes out is a claim. Keep a wall between them. The trap is crossing it, by testing a lead on the data that suggested it. Friday was picked because it looked best in these very bills... so the test is tilted its way before it runs. A p-value from the data that suggested the question is a lie. So where does the fresh data come from?

If you can't collect more, split what you have before you explore. Seventy percent to roam in... and thirty locked away. When a lead turns up, carry the question across the wall, but not the data. Then test it once, on bills that never had a say in the hunch. Or better still, make fresh data on purpose.

That's an A/B test: an experiment where almost everything is decided before the first user arrives. One hypothesis. The new checkout button raises the conversion rate. And one metric to judge it by, chosen now. Track ten and cheer whichever one moves, and you're back to forking paths. Then comes the step that makes it an experiment.
